messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marvin, a thirty‑year‑old African‑American curriculum designer, had once found comfort in the orderly cadence of lesson plans and the quiet hum of his office’s fluorescent lights. The life he had known—a single, focused professional life—was shattered that spring when a physical altercation with his then‑girlfriend turned his home into a scene of violence. The night of the attack, she struck him repeatedly in the ribs and jaw while drunk, her breath heavy with the stench of alcohol. He remembered the hot, acrid smell of burning plastic from the fire alarm that had blared moments earlier, the sharp sting of smoke on his tongue, and the sharp, metallic taste of blood on his lips. Those sensations were etched into his memory alongside the raw terror he felt, a terror that felt all the more real when the smoke was still in the air. The pain was not just psychological; he could feel the exact same ache in his ribs and jaw when the memory surfaced. A year later, Marvin began noticing that the scent of a colleague’s cologne—containing a faint hint of the same alcohol he had once inhaled—could suddenly trigger a flood of old memories. In meetings, when a coworker joked about family dinners, the words “family” landed like a hammer on his ears, pulling him back into the night of the assault. The combination of those family‑related comments and the lingering odor of alcohol in the office space forced his mind to relive the event, and each time the memory returned, the physical pain in his ribs and the panic that had driven him to the emergency room resurfaced with unnerving clarity. The very triggers that had been benign for years became the doorways to a painful past. The vividness of those memories did more than simply bring pain. As he recalled the night, the terror he once felt swelled into a full‑scale panic that left him trembling and heart racing. The same scenes that had once been confined to the darkness of that night now erupted whenever he smelled burnt plastic, smelled alcohol, or heard family gossip in the office corridor. Each time a trigger appeared, the memory rushed forward so forcefully that it seemed as though the past had leapt out of its temporal bounds and into his present, a loop that pulled him deeper into the same emotional landscape. Marvin’s struggle was not limited to the physical sensations of the memory. The recollection of the assault forced him to confront a new self‑image that he felt was utterly unrecognizable. He could no longer see the calm, dependable man who had designed curriculum and met deadlines; instead, he saw a man who felt forever dirty, as if the violent assault had smeared an invisible stain across his entire being. He was consumed by a sense of injustice, convinced that the world had failed him and that no one had done anything to right the wrong that had been inflicted upon him. The injustice, the contamination, and the alienation from his own identity fed into each other, creating a relentless cycle of self‑denigration that lingered long after the memory had faded. The same triggers that opened the floodgate to memory also amplified Marvin’s negative appraisals. Every time a coworker, in casual conversation, mentioned a family holiday or a mother’s anniversary, Marvin could not help but feel that these references were a reminder that his past had been discarded, that he was no longer the person he had once been. The presence of alcohol in the office, even if only a faint whiff, amplified his belief that he was forever tainted, that society had left him in the shadows of shame. The combination of these triggers and the weight of his negative thoughts made Marvin feel that he could never fully reintegrate into his professional sphere or rebuild the identity he had lost. Today, Marvin sits at his desk surrounded by stacks of worksheets and student feedback, the office hum a constant backdrop to his inner turmoil. He no longer feels at ease when a colleague speaks about their family, and the smell of after‑shave in the break room makes his chest tighten as though he were again on the brink of an assault. In the months since the assault, his productivity has slipped; he often arrives late to meetings, and his once‑reliable project deadlines have become sporadic. He has been avoiding conversations about family and has kept his personal life under wraps, a self‑imposed isolation that has left him feeling increasingly alienated from his own colleagues. It is this spiraling sense of being stuck, of never escaping the phantom presence of violence and the guilt of an unrecognizable self, that finally led him to seek help. He hopes to reclaim the calm that once guided his lesson plans, and he fears that if he does not break this cycle, he will forever live in the shadows of that night.
